title: Hands Fold a Paper Sheet
tests: Tests coherent hand anatomy, hand-object contact and a completed paper-folding action in one text-generated shot.

faults.what: The paper develops diagonal, envelope-like flaps and additional folds instead of remaining a simple sheet folded once in half; these are especially visible at 5 and 7 seconds.
The sheet already has multiple pronounced vertical folds at 1 second rather than appearing as a plain, initially unfolded sheet.

judge.summary: The realistic overhead clip shows plausible hands folding and smoothing blue paper, but the extra folds and envelope-like result depart from the requested simple half-fold.

must_haves.item: Both human hands and the entire blue sheet remain visible on a wooden table.
must_haves.why: Both hands and the paper stay within the frame in all supplied views, with a wooden tabletop underneath.

must_haves.item: The hands visibly bring one half of the sheet over the other, producing a folded sheet rather than an abrupt object replacement.
must_haves.why: The paper is partly open at 1 second and closed by 3 seconds, but the sampled frames do not show the intervening movement well enough to verify a continuous half-fold.

must_haves.item: The hands press along the resulting crease after folding.
must_haves.why: The 3- and 5-second views show the hands pressing and smoothing the folded paper.

must_haves.item: Hands remain anatomically plausible, without extra or fused fingers, and make convincing contact with the paper.
must_haves.why: The visible hands have plausible anatomy and appear to grip or press the paper naturally.

must_haves.item: The blue paper remains a single consistent object throughout the action.
must_haves.why: It remains one blue paper object in the supplied views, although it acquires unwanted additional folds.

must_haves.item: The eight-second widescreen video uses one fixed overhead shot and has no sound.
must_haves.why: The supplied frames are consistent with a fixed widescreen overhead shot, and the clip is identified as eight seconds long, but silence cannot be verified from still images.
